newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Copper still flooding into LME warehouses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Copper still flooding into LME warehouses.

text.p: Large quantities of copper continued to arrive in London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses, but it appeared to have been expected and prices actually finished Thursday with moderate gains.
Elsewhere in commodity markets Egypt announced a ban on imports of genetically modified grains.

In the copper market a further 13,025 tonnes of the red metal was delivered into LME approved warehouses, following the 17,025 tonnes on Wednesday, and some traders were saying that a total of upto 100,000 tonnes could arrive by mid-August.

High premiums for prompt delivery copper on the LME was attracting surplus metal from some south-east Asian markets where demand has not been as strong as expected, and also from other warehouses in the U.S.
Late in the day workers at Portugal's 107,000 tonnes a year Neves Corvo copper mine rejected renewed company proposals for seven-day shift working.
But although this was supportive, miners were not expected to renew last week's strike action immediately.

Copper prices on the LME dipped to $2,226, a five-month low, before rallying strongly to end the afternoon at $2,280, up $13 from Wednesday, as a bout of consumer buying and shortcovering was attracted by the cheaper levels.

Grain markets in Chicago were relatively stable and watching the weather situation in the U.S. Midwest but elsewhere, Egypt hit the grain world with a decree on genetically modified grain/soy imports.

Local traders in Egypt were sent the decree this week which said that "it is not approved to import foodstuffs which have used genetic engineering in their production, until they are proven fit for consumption."
The U.S. Department of Agriculture said they were pressing for a meeting with Egyptian officials, saying they were "very concerned."
Genetically modified agricultural products have been a target for environmentalists but U.S. farmers are keen to develop export markets.

In soft commodities coffee lost ground in rather slow trading with traders gradually accepting the likelihood their would be no crop-damaging frost in Brazil this year. Cocoa was also lower as investors liquidated some of their holdings.
